q.t: Which of these statements is correct?
q.e: In 1284 King Edward I of England introduced the Statute of Rhuddlan, which annexed Wales to the Crown of England. During the reign of Henry VIII, Wales became formally united with England by the Act for the Government of Wales, and the Welsh sent representatives to the House of Commons.
o: Wales became formally united with England by the Act for the Government of Wales
Wales became formally united with England by the Statute of Rhuddlan

q.t: Which TWO castles were built to maintain English power in Wales?
q.e: In 1284 King Edward I of England introduced the Statute of Rhuddlan, which annexed Wales to the Crown of England. Huge castles, including Conwy and Caernarvon, were built to maintain this power.

q.t: By 1400, in what language were official documents in England being written?
q.e: Gradually these two languages combined to become one English language. By 1400, in England, official documents were being written in English, and English had become the preferred language of the royal court and Parliament.

q.t: Which work by Geoffrey Chaucer was one of the first books to be printed by William Caxton?
q.e: In the years leading up to 1400, Geoffrey Chaucer wrote a series of poems in English about a group of people going to Canterbury on a pilgrimage. This collection of poems is called The Canterbury Tales. It was one of the first books to be printed by William Caxton.
o: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight

q.t: Which TWO cathedrals are named in the handbook in connection with the Middle Ages?
q.e: Great cathedrals, for example Lincoln Cathedral, were also built, and many of these are still used for worship. Several of the cathedrals had windows of stained glass. The glass in York Minster is a famous example.

q.t: What became a very important English export during the Middle Ages?
q.e: During this period, England was an important trading nation. English wool became a very important export. People came to England from abroad to trade and also to work.

q.t: Which skilled workers came to England from Holland during the Middle Ages?
q.e: Many had special skills, such as weavers from France, engineers from Germany, glass manufacturers from Italy and canal builders from Holland.

q.t: Which TWO castles from the Middle Ages are still in use today, according to the handbook?
q.e: Castles were built in many places in Britain and Ireland, partly for defence. Today many are in ruins, although some, such as Windsor and Edinburgh, are still in use.

q.t: Under feudalism, what did the king give to his lords, and what did he receive in return?
q.e: The Normans used a system of land ownership known as feudalism. The king gave land to his lords in return for help in war. Landowners had to send certain numbers of men to serve in the army.
o: He gave land in return for help in war
He gave money in return for taxes
He gave castles in return for wool
He gave titles in return for land

q.t: In which parts of Britain and Ireland was land owned by 'clans' rather than under feudalism?
q.e: Some peasants had their own land but most were serfs. The same system developed in southern Scotland. In the north of Scotland and Ireland, land was owned by members of the 'clans', prominent families.
o: The north of Scotland and Ireland

q.t: Which TWO new social groups emerged following the Black Death?
q.e: Following the Black Death, the smaller population meant there was less need to grow cereal crops. There were labour shortages and peasants began to demand higher wages. New social classes appeared, including owners of large areas of land, later called the gentry, and people left the countryside to live in the towns. In the towns, growing wealth led to the development of a strong middle class.

q.t: Which of these statements is correct?
q.e: This war was called the Wars of the Roses, because the symbol of Lancaster was a red rose and the symbol of York was a white rose. The war ended with the Battle of Bosworth Field in 1485.
o: The symbol of the House of Lancaster was a red rose
The symbol of the House of Lancaster was a white rose

q.t: Whom did Henry VII marry in order to unite the two families after Bosworth Field?
q.e: King Richard III of the House of York was killed in the battle and Henry Tudor, the leader of the House of Lancaster, became King Henry VII. Henry then married King Richard's niece, Elizabeth of York, and united the two families.
o: Elizabeth of York, King Richard's niece

q.t: What was the symbol of the House of Tudor?
q.e: Henry was the first king of the House of Tudor. The symbol of the House of Tudor was a red rose with a white rose inside it as a sign that the Houses of York and Lancaster were now allies.
o: A red rose with a white rose inside it
A white rose with a red rose inside it

q.t: Which TWO things did Henry VII do after winning the Wars of the Roses?
q.e: Henry VII won the Wars of the Roses, curbed the power of the nobles and built up the treasury. When he died, his son Henry VIII continued centralising power.
o: He curbed the power of the nobles
He created the Church of England
He annexed Wales to the Crown of England

q.t: Which of these did Protestants do, according to the handbook's account of the Reformation?
q.e: The Protestants formed their own churches. They read the Bible in their own languages instead of in Latin; they did not pray to saints or at shrines; and they believed that a person's own relationship with God was more important than submitting to the authority of the Church.
o: They read the Bible in their own languages instead of in Latin
They prayed to saints and at shrines
They accepted the authority of the Pope
They read the Bible only in Latin

q.t: What is the King James Version of the Bible also known as?
q.e: One achievement of King James' reign was a new translation of the Bible into English. This translation is known as the 'King James Version' or the 'Authorised Version'. It was not the first English Bible but is a version which continues to be used in many Protestant churches today.

q.t:
Is the statement below TRUE or FALSE?
When James VI of Scotland became King James I of England, Scotland remained a separate country.
q.e: Elizabeth I never married and so had no children of her own to inherit her throne. When she died in 1603 her heir was her cousin James VI of Scotland. He became King James I of England, Wales and Ireland but Scotland remained a separate country.

q.t: Who were the Puritans?
q.e: Many in Parliament were Puritans, a group of Protestants who advocated strict and simple religious doctrine and worship. They did not agree with the king's religious views and disliked his reforms of the Church of England.
o: A group of Protestants who advocated strict and simple religious doctrine and worship
A group of Catholics who supported the Pope
Supporters of the king in the civil war
Followers of Oliver Cromwell in Ireland

q.t: Which battle did William III win in Ireland in 1690?
q.e: James II wanted to regain the throne and invaded Ireland with the help of a French army. William defeated James II at the Battle of the Boyne in Ireland in 1690, an event which is still celebrated by some in Northern Ireland today.

q.t: Why was the revolution of 1688 called the 'Glorious Revolution'?
q.e: This event was later called the 'Glorious Revolution' because there was no fighting in England and because it guaranteed the power of Parliament, ending the threat of a monarch ruling on his or her own as he or she wished.
o: There was no fighting in England and it guaranteed the power of Parliament
It restored the Catholic faith in England
It gave every man the right to vote

q.t: What happened to the MacDonalds of Glencoe?
q.e: All Scottish clans were required formally to accept William as king by taking an oath. The MacDonalds of Glencoe were late in taking the oath and were all killed. The memory of this massacre meant some Scots distrusted the new government.
o: They were all killed for being late in taking the oath to William
They were exiled to France with James II
They were given land in Ulster

q.t: What were the supporters of James II known as?
q.e: Some continued to believe that James was the rightful king, particularly in Scotland. Some joined him in exile in France; others were secret supporters. James' supporters became known as Jacobites.

q.t: Which of these statements is correct?
q.e: James II's elder daughter, Mary, was married to her cousin William of Orange, the Protestant ruler of the Netherlands. William took over the throne, becoming William III in England, Wales and Ireland, and William II of Scotland. He ruled jointly with Mary.
o: William of Orange became William III in England and William II in Scotland
William of Orange became William II in England and William III in Scotland
